n11-licao-projetos.enunciado:
Each project has 5 stages. Each stage starts from your files from the previous stage (if you did it; if not, from the reference solution) and asks for something new. The tests apply all the files to a fresh cluster, so everything you’ve built has to keep working.

  • The full store: API, Redis, the storefront and the way in through the Ingress.
  • The blog with a database: Secret, a StatefulSet with a disk and the backup.
  • Zero-downtime deploy: readiness, the rolling update strategy and a PDB.
  • Canary: two versions and the traffic split through the Gateway API.
  • Black Friday: requests and limits, the HPA under load, the quota and the LimitRange.
  • Multi-team: one namespace per team, RBAC, quotas and NetworkPolicy.
  • Hardening: no root, no privileges, a read-only disk, Pod Security and least access.
  • Dev and prod: the same store in two environments, with Helm and with Kustomize.

A tip from people who do this every day: kubectl apply -f ., kubectl get all and kubectl describe solve almost everything. When you get stuck, the Solution tab has the reference for each stage.
n11-licao-projetos.vidaReal: Until now, each mission was a single room. Now it’s the whole construction job: foundation, walls, plumbing and finishing, one stage after another.
n11-licao-projetos.limite: On a real job, nobody rebuilds the foundation at every stage. Here, the tests set everything up again on a clean cluster: whatever you forgot in one stage shows up in the next.

n11-loja-1.titulo: The API and its phone extension
n11-loja-1.enunciado: api.yaml has the API Deployment with 1 replica. Bump it to 2 replicas and add the api Service (port 80, to the pods’ 8080).
n11-loja-1.dica: replicas: 2 and, in the same file after a ---, the Service with selector app: api, port 80 and targetPort 8080.
n11-loja-1.vidaReal: First, the service counter (the API) and the fixed phone extension to reach it.
n11-loja-1.limite: The phone extension only exists for people inside the condo: from outside, nobody can get in yet.

testes.descricao: the API answers on its phone extension

n11-loja-2.enunciado: redis.yaml has the Redis Deployment. Add the redis Service (port 6379) and, in api.yaml, the REDIS_HOST=redis variable on the API.
n11-loja-2.dica: Service redis: port 6379, targetPort 6379. On the API: env: [{ name: REDIS_HOST, value: redis }].
n11-loja-2.vidaReal: The API gets a fridge (Redis) so it doesn’t have to fetch everything from the stockroom every time.
n11-loja-2.limite: The fridge’s address is written into the API (REDIS_HOST): renaming the Service breaks the link.

testes.descricao: the API knows where the cache is

n11-loja-3.enunciado: vitrine.yaml (the storefront) has nginx mounting the vitrine-html ConfigMap, which doesn’t exist. Create the ConfigMap with an index.html containing Loja do kube-learn, and the vitrine Service (port 80).
n11-loja-3.dica:
ConfigMap vitrine-html with data: { index.html: "

Loja do kube-learn

" } and the vitrine Service (port 80, targetPort 80).
n11-loja-3.vidaReal: The storefront (nginx) shows the page pinned on the bulletin board (the ConfigMap).
n11-loja-3.limite: nginx reads the file from the volume on every request: changing the ConfigMap changes the page a few seconds later, with no restart.

n11-loja-4.enunciado: entrada.yaml sends loja.local to the storefront. Add the /api path to the api Service.
n11-loja-4.dica: One more item in paths: path /api, pathType Prefix, backend service api, port 80.
n11-loja-4.vidaReal: The front gate’s front desk: whoever asks for “loja.local” goes to the storefront; whoever asks for “/api” goes to the API counter.
n11-loja-4.limite: The Ingress picks the longest path: /api beats / for anyone asking for /api/anything.

n11-loja-5.enunciado: On the API: a readinessProbe on /healthz (port 8080) and requests of 100m CPU and 64Mi memory. On the storefront: a readinessProbe on / (port 80). An API update must not leave anyone hanging.
n11-loja-5.dica: readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } } and resources: { requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi } }.
n11-loja-5.vidaReal: Before opening the doors: the building manager checks who’s ready, and each clerk says how much power they need.
n11-loja-5.limite: The readinessProbe only protects you if the answer is honest: a /healthz that always says ok protects against nothing.

testes.descricao: the probes and the requests are in place
the API switches versions without anyone going unanswered

n11-blog-1.enunciado: segredo.yaml has the empty banco (database) Secret. Put the senha (password) key in it (any value you like).
n11-blog-1.vidaReal: Before calling in the database, the sealed envelope with the password.
n11-blog-1.limite: Sealed isn’t a safe: anyone who can read Secrets in the namespace can read the password (it’s just base64).

n11-blog-2.enunciado: banco.yaml has the db StatefulSet (postgres), which crashes without a password. Give it POSTGRES_PASSWORD read from the banco Secret and create the headless Service db (port 5432).
n11-blog-2.dica: env with valueFrom.secretKeyRef (name: banco, key: senha) and a Service with clusterIP: None.
n11-blog-2.vidaReal: The database’s apartment 0, with a fixed number, and the list with each apartment’s direct extension (the headless Service), which calls it by name.
n11-blog-2.limite: Headless doesn’t spread the calls around: it only gives out each apartment’s address (db-0.db).

n11-blog-3.enunciado: Give the database its own disk: a volumeClaimTemplates dados (data) of 1Gi, mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data.
n11-blog-3.dica: volumeClaimTemplates in the StatefulSet spec and the volumeMount with the same name (dados).
n11-blog-3.vidaReal: Apartment 0 gets its own storage unit in the garage: if the resident changes, the unit keeps its stuff.
n11-blog-3.limite: Deleting the StatefulSet doesn’t delete the storage unit (the PVC): the data stays until someone deletes the PVC.

testes.descricao: the database has its own disk
db-0 comes back with the same disk (and the data)

msgs.0: the file written earlier is still there

n11-blog-4.enunciado: blog.yaml has the blog Deployment. Give it the variables DB_HOST=db-0.db and DB_SENHA (from the banco Secret), and create the blog Service (port 80).
n11-blog-4.dica: env: DB_HOST with value and DB_SENHA with valueFrom.secretKeyRef; Service blog: port 80, targetPort 80.
n11-blog-4.vidaReal: The blog lives in another apartment and calls the database at apartment 0’s fixed address, with the password from the envelope.
n11-blog-4.limite: The db-0.db address always points to the same pod: if the database got replicas, the blog wouldn’t talk to them.

msgs.3: DB_SENHA comes from the banco Secret

n11-blog-5.enunciado: backup.yaml has the backup-db CronJob running every minute (for testing). Change it to every day at 2 AM.
n11-blog-5.vidaReal: Every night, at 2 AM, someone copies the database into the safe.
n11-blog-5.limite: A backup that’s never been tested isn’t a backup: run the Job by hand every now and then.

testes.descricao: the backup runs every day at 2 AM

n11-zero-1.titulo: The store and its phone extension
n11-zero-1.enunciado: loja.yaml has the store Deployment (4 replicas). Add the loja Service (port 80 → 8080).
n11-zero-1.dica: Service with selector app: loja, port 80 and targetPort 8080.
n11-zero-1.vidaReal: Four clerks and the store’s fixed phone extension.
n11-zero-1.limite: For now, the phone extension sends customers to any clerk who’s up, ready or not.

n11-zero-2.enunciado: Add a readinessProbe on /healthz (port 8080). The hidden tests swap the store for a version that takes a while to warm up.
n11-zero-2.vidaReal: The store’s new version takes 20 seconds to warm up. Without asking whether it’s ready, the phone extension sends customers to clerks still tying their aprons.
n11-zero-2.limite: Readiness doesn’t speed anything up: the clerk still takes just as long, they just don’t get anyone before they’re ready.

testes.descricao: the warming-up version doesn’t drop anyone

n11-zero-3.enunciado: Configure the rolling update to never drop below 4 ready pods: maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1.
n11-zero-3.dica: spec.strategy: { type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 } }
n11-zero-3.vidaReal: In a step-by-step renovation, a new apartment opens before an old one closes: never fewer than 4 open.
n11-zero-3.limite: Without room for the extra apartment (the maxSurge), the renovation stalls: maxUnavailable 0 needs spare capacity in the cluster.

n11-zero-4.enunciado: Create a pdb.yaml with a PodDisruptionBudget loja that guarantees at least 3 ready pods.
n11-zero-4.dica: policy/v1, kind PodDisruptionBudget, spec: { minAvailable: 3, selector: { matchLabels: { app: loja } } }
n11-zero-4.vidaReal: During building maintenance (the drain), at least 3 clerks keep serving.
n11-zero-4.limite: The PDB doesn’t hold up against a power outage: only planned departures (drain).

testes.descricao: the PDB lets them leave one at a time

n11-zero-5.titulo: The new version, with a name
n11-zero-5.enunciado: Update the store to version 1.1 and note the reason on the Deployment (kubernetes.io/change-cause: "versão 1.1"), so it shows up in kubectl rollout history. Everything you did before still applies.
n11-zero-5.dica: The Deployment’s metadata.annotations and image: kubelearn/loja:1.1.
n11-zero-5.vidaReal: The renovation gets a sign (“version 1.1”) so everyone knows what changed, and it can be undone.
n11-zero-5.limite: The change-cause is just an annotation: write the truth, because the history shows whatever is there.

testes.descricao: the next update doesn’t drop anyone either

n11-canario-1.enunciado: v1.yaml has loja-v1 (3 replicas, labels app: loja and versao: v1). Create the loja-v1 Service that selects only the v1 pods.
n11-canario-1.vidaReal: The usual store, with the version tag on each apartment’s door.
n11-canario-1.limite: The versao label is just a tag: Kubernetes doesn’t know what a version is; the selectors are what use it.

testes.descricao: v1 answers on its own phone extension

n11-canario-2.enunciado: v2.yaml has loja-v2 (version 1.1, 1 replica, versao: v2). Create the loja-v2 Service, selecting only v2.
n11-canario-2.dica: The same Service as v1, with versao: v2.
n11-canario-2.vidaReal: A single apartment with the new renovation, to see if anyone complains before renovating the whole building.
n11-canario-2.limite: A canary with few visitors takes a while to show defects: give it time (and traffic) before deciding.

testes.descricao: each version with its own phone extension

n11-canario-3.enunciado: rota.yaml sends everything from loja.local to v1. Split it: 90 to loja-v1 and 10 to loja-v2.
n11-canario-3.dica: backendRefs: [{ name: loja-v1, port: 80, weight: 90 }, { name: loja-v2, port: 80, weight: 10 }]
n11-canario-3.vidaReal: The sign at the front gate sends 1 in every 10 visitors to the renovated apartment.
n11-canario-3.limite: The weight is per connection, not per person: the same customer may land on one version now and the other later.

n11-canario-4.enunciado: Switch to 50/50 and, since v2 is going to get many more visitors, scale loja-v2 up to 3 replicas.
n11-canario-4.dica: weight: 50 on both and replicas: 3 in v2.yaml.
n11-canario-4.vidaReal: Nobody complained: half the visitors already go to the renovation.
n11-canario-4.limite: Half and half with 3 pods on one side and 1 on the other: the v2 pod gets the same load as the 3 v1 pods combined.

n11-canario-5.enunciado: Send all the traffic to v2 and shut down v1 (remove v1.yaml and take v1 out of the route).
n11-canario-5.dica: A rule with only loja-v2 (weight 100, or no weight) and delete the v1.yaml file.
n11-canario-5.vidaReal: The renovation was approved: everyone moves to the new apartments, and the old ones close.
n11-canario-5.limite: Once v1 is deleted, going back means bringing v1 up again: keep its YAML until you’re sure.

n11-bf-1.enunciado: Give the store requests of 100m CPU and 64Mi memory and limits of 500m and 128Mi.
n11-bf-1.dica: resources: { requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi }, limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 128Mi } }
n11-bf-1.vidaReal: Before Black Friday, each clerk says how much power they need (request) and the most they can draw (limit).
n11-bf-1.limite: The request is a reservation, not a measurement: the pod may use less (waste) or more (up to the limit).

n11-bf-2.enunciado: hpa.yaml has a timid HPA. Adjust it: minimum 2, maximum 8, target of 50% CPU.
n11-bf-2.vidaReal: The temp-staff manager hires temps when the clerks go past half their capacity, and lets them go afterward.
n11-bf-2.limite: They only look at CPU: if the bottleneck is the database, hiring clerks doesn’t help.

n11-bf-3.enunciado: trafego.yaml has the carga (load) pod, a client that hits the store nonstop, but the address is wrong (check its logs). Fix it and watch the HPA grow (kubectl get hpa -w, with about +30s).
n11-bf-3.dica: kubectl logs carga (bad address). The Service is named loja: http://loja
n11-bf-3.vidaReal: Customers pour in: the manager sees the clerks at their limit and calls in the temps.
n11-bf-3.limite: The HPA reacts, it doesn’t predict: the first minutes of the sale still catch the store small.

msgs.1: the HPA asked for more than 2 replicas

n11-bf-4.enunciado: Apply the teto (cap) quota from cota.yaml. With a CPU and memory quota, every container needs requests and limits: give the carga pod requests of 50m and 16Mi and limits of 100m and 32Mi.
n11-bf-4.dica: trafego.yaml gets resources; the quota is already done. kubectl applies the files in alphabetical order: the quota (cota.yaml) arrives before the pod.
n11-bf-4.vidaReal: The management office put a cap on the company’s power: and, with a cap, every appliance that comes in needs an energy label.
n11-bf-4.limite: The quota turns away anything that arrives without a label, even the test client: that’s why it comes together with the LimitRange.

n11-bf-5.enunciado: tarefa.yaml is a pod without resources, rejected by the quota. Instead of touching it, create a LimitRange padrao (default) with a defaultRequest of 50m and 32Mi and a default (limits) of 100m and 64Mi.
n11-bf-5.dica: kind: LimitRange, spec.limits: [{ type: Container, defaultRequest: {...}, default: {...} }]. The LimitRange has to exist before the pod: put it in cota.yaml.
n11-bf-5.vidaReal: So it doesn’t turn away whoever forgets the label, the management office sticks a default label on anyone who arrives without one.
n11-bf-5.limite: The default only applies to new pods: those already running don’t get the label.

testes.descricao: the task got the default and got in

n11-equipes-1.enunciado: andares.yaml creates the time-a and time-b namespaces, and time-a.yaml puts team A’s API (Deployment and Service) on its floor. time-b.yaml is empty: write team B’s API and Service, the same as team A’s.
n11-equipes-1.dica: Copy time-a.yaml, changing the namespace to time-b.
n11-equipes-1.vidaReal: Each team rents a floor (the namespace), with its own API and its own phone extension.
n11-equipes-1.limite: A floor alone doesn’t isolate anything: without badges and turnstiles, anyone can walk all over.

n11-equipes-2.enunciado: crachas.yaml gives ana the dev role in time-a. Do the same for bruno in time-b.
n11-equipes-2.dica: A Role dev and a RoleBinding dev-bruno in the time-b namespace.
n11-equipes-2.vidaReal: The user ana has the floor A badge; bruno, the floor B one. Neither opens the other’s door.
n11-equipes-2.limite: The dev badge lets you delete everything on the floor: for someone who only looks, a read-only badge.

testes.descricao: each one on their own floor

n11-equipes-3.enunciado: cotas.yaml limits time-a to 5 pods. Do the same for time-b.
n11-equipes-3.dica: Another ResourceQuota cota, in the time-b namespace, with hard.pods: "5".
n11-equipes-3.vidaReal: Each team can have up to 5 apartments in the condo.
n11-equipes-3.limite: The quota counts the pods that exist: a rollout with maxSurge needs room for the extra pod.

n11-equipes-4.titulo: Each one on their own floor
n11-equipes-4.enunciado: catracas.yaml closes time-a to outsiders (only pods from its own namespace get through). Do the same for time-b. clientes.yaml puts a client on each floor for the tests.
n11-equipes-4.dica: The same so-o-andar NetworkPolicy in the time-b namespace.
n11-equipes-4.vidaReal: Each floor’s turnstiles only let in people from that same floor.
n11-equipes-4.limite: Whoever has the floor’s badge (RBAC) can change its turnstiles: turnstiles are network, badges are API.

testes.descricao: each one on their own floor

n11-equipes-5.enunciado: Let the time-a pods call the time-b API (a namespaceSelector on team B’s turnstile). The other way around stays closed.
n11-equipes-5.dica: In time-b’s so-o-andar: one more item in from, with namespaceSelector { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: time-a }.
n11-equipes-5.vidaReal: Team B opens its API’s door to team A (and only to them).
n11-equipes-5.limite: Opening to the whole floor opens to any pod team A creates there: tighten it with a podSelector if you need to.

testes.descricao: A calls B; B doesn’t call A

n11-cofre-1.titulo: The safe without the master key
n11-cofre-1.enunciado: Make cofre (the safe) run as user 1000 and refuse root (runAsNonRoot), in the pod’s securityContext.
n11-cofre-1.vidaReal: The safe’s program runs with an ordinary resident’s key, never with the master key.
n11-cofre-1.limite: Running without root limits the damage, but it doesn’t replace updating the image with the security fixes.

n11-cofre-2.enunciado: On the container: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]. On the pod: seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault.
n11-cofre-2.dica: Look back at the safe’s fire-code project (level 8): these are exactly the restricted fields.
n11-cofre-2.vidaReal: Besides not having the master key, the resident can’t borrow one (privilege escalation), and gives up the special tools.
n11-cofre-2.limite: The RuntimeDefault seccomp profile blocks rare system calls: an unusual program may need a profile of its own.

n11-cofre-3.enunciado: A read-only container disk (readOnlyRootFilesystem) and an emptyDir at /tmp.
n11-cofre-3.dica: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in the container’s securityContext; volumes: [{ name: tmp, emptyDir: {} }] and the volumeMount at /tmp.
n11-cofre-3.vidaReal: The safe’s walls stay sealed; the program only writes on the workbench (/tmp).
n11-cofre-3.limite: /tmp is an emptyDir: whatever is there disappears when the pod goes away.

n11-cofre-4.enunciado: bloco.yaml creates the cofre namespace with enforce=restricted. Move the Deployment into that namespace.
n11-cofre-4.vidaReal: The safe moves into the block with the fire marshals’ strictest code: since it’s already up to code, it gets in without trouble.
n11-cofre-4.limite: The code only checks new pods: an old pod, created before the label, keeps running.

testes.descricao: the safe passed the fire marshals’ inspection

n11-cofre-5.enunciado: isola.yaml creates the cofre ServiceAccount (no token) and a NetworkPolicy that blocks ingress and egress. Make the Deployment use that ServiceAccount, without mounting the token (automountServiceAccountToken: false).
n11-cofre-5.dica: In the pod spec: serviceAccountName: cofre and automountServiceAccountToken: false.
n11-cofre-5.vidaReal: The safe doesn’t need to talk to the management office: it goes without a machine badge, and the turnstiles close its way in and out.
n11-cofre-5.limite: With no way out at all, not even DNS works: if the program needs something from outside, allow just that.

n11-ambientes-1.enunciado: dev.yaml has the dev values. From the terminal, install the loja-dev release of kube-learn/loja with them, in the dev namespace (which doesn’t exist yet).
n11-ambientes-1.dica: helm install loja-dev kube-learn/loja -f dev.yaml -n dev --create-namespace
n11-ambientes-1.vidaReal: The builder’s same standard design, with each city’s finishes in a file.
n11-ambientes-1.limite: Each environment’s values.yaml is code: keep it in git, along with everything else.
n11-ambientes-1.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-ambientes-2.enunciado: Finish prod.yaml: 3 replicas, tag "1.1" and the Ingress turned on with the host loja.prod. Install the loja-prod release in the prod namespace.
n11-ambientes-2.dica: replicaCount, image.tag and ingress: { enabled: true, host: loja.prod }. helm install loja-prod kube-learn/loja -f prod.yaml -n prod --create-namespace
n11-ambientes-2.vidaReal: The big branch: more clerks, the new version and a desk out on the street.
n11-ambientes-2.limite: Two values files drift apart over time: whatever doesn’t need to differ, leave it at the chart’s defaults.
n11-ambientes-2.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-ambientes-3.enunciado: The base/ folder has the store’s Deployment and Service, but base/kustomization.yaml doesn’t list anything yet. List both under resources. The overlays/dev overlay already uses the base.
n11-ambientes-3.vidaReal: Another team prefers the common blueprint with adjustment sheets: the base is plain YAML.
n11-ambientes-3.limite: Helm and Kustomize together on the same object fight each other: pick one per application.

testes.descricao: the dev overlay builds the base

n11-ambientes-3.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-ambientes-4.enunciado: The overlays/prod overlay only puts together the base and the prod-k namespace. Finish its kustomization.yaml: everything in the prod-k namespace, 3 replicas and the image at tag 1.1. Use the dev one as a model.
n11-ambientes-4.dica: resources: [../../base, namespace.yaml], namespace: prod-k, replicas: [{ name: loja, count: 3 }], images: [{ name: kubelearn/loja, newTag: "1.1" }]
n11-ambientes-4.vidaReal: The big branch’s adjustment sheet: its neighborhood, more clerks and the new version.
n11-ambientes-4.limite: Overlays only see the base: an adjustment everyone wants goes in the base, not copied into every sheet.
n11-ambientes-4.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-ambientes-5.enunciado: Make the base read the loja-config ConfigMap (an envFrom on the Deployment) and generate that ConfigMap in each overlay: COR=amarelo in dev and COR=azul in prod.
n11-ambientes-5.dica: In the base: envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: loja-config } }]. In each overlay: configMapGenerator: [{ name: loja-config, literals: [COR=...] }].
n11-ambientes-5.vidaReal: Each branch paints its storefront a different color: each one’s bulletin board is generated from its own sheet.
n11-ambientes-5.limite: The hash changes the ConfigMap’s name on every change: anything using the fixed name somewhere else (a script) gets lost.
n11-ambientes-5.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-licao-proximos-passos.enunciado:
Everything you did here works on a real cluster: the commands and the YAMLs are the same. Three ways to get started, from the simplest to the most complete:

Killercoda (in the browser)

A real cluster, free, for an hour, with nothing to install: killercoda.com/playgrounds. Good for redoing the missions from here with real containers.

kind (on your computer)

The same one that checked this site’s outputs: a cluster inside Docker.

# with Docker installed
kind create cluster --name estudo
kubectl get nodes
kubectl apply -f loja.yaml
kind delete cluster --name estudo

For 3 nodes like here, a config file with one control-plane and two worker.

minikube

Another local cluster, with ready-made extras (minikube addons enable metrics-server, minikube dashboard). Watch out for the ingress addon: it installs ingress-nginx, retired in 2026 (level 3). For the front gate, prefer the Gateway API: install its CRDs and an implementation, such as Envoy Gateway or Traefik.

Where to go next

  • The official documentation: kubernetes.io/docs.
  • If you want a certification, the CKAD covers almost everything on this path (the exam is hands-on, in a terminal, with access to the documentation).
  • Build your own project: take an application of yours and write the manifests from scratch. That’s where you see what you’ve learned.

Thanks for coming aboard. The ship is fully loaded. 🚢
n11-licao-proximos-passos.vidaReal: You trained in the model condo. Now it’s time to visit a real construction site: the same kubectl, the same YAMLs, only with real containers running.
n11-licao-proximos-passos.limite: The simulator mimicked kubectl’s output against a real kind, but it’s a simulator: on a real cluster, images take time, networks fail in new ways and errors don’t come with an explanation underneath.
